admin_user_toggle performs a state-changing operation (enabling/disabling user accounts) via a GET request (linked with in templates). Django's CsrfViewMiddleware does not protect GET requests, so an attacker can embed e.g. on a third-party page to CSRF an admin into disabling a user account.

assignment_status changes assignment status (publish/close/archive) via a GET request triggered by <a href> links. GET requests are not protected by Django's CSRF middleware, allowing cross-site request forgery of assignment state transitions.
release_grade releases a grade to a student via a GET request triggered by an <a href> link. Because GET is exempt from CSRF protection, an attacker can forge a request to release grades prematurely.

discussion_moderate changes thread status (pin/lock/hide/open) via a GET request through <a href> links. GET requests are exempt from Django CSRF checks, allowing cross-site forgery of moderation actions.

request_resubmission changes a submission's status to needs_resubmission via a GET request triggered by an <a href> link. GET requests are not protected by Django's CSRF middleware, allowing cross-site forgery.
The response explicitly sets `X-XSS-Protection: 0` and an empty `Content-Security-Policy`, disabling two important browser-side defenses and weakening XSS protections.
Hardcoded verifier/credential values are embedded in source: `known = {"north": "4812", "south": "5930"}`. These static secrets are used for handle verification and can be extracted from the code.

SECRET_KEY falls back to the hardcoded value "django-insecure-local-dev-only" when the environment variable is not set. If deployed without setting SECRET_KEY, the known key allows session forgery, CSRF token bypass, and signing attacks.

Demo accounts are created with hardcoded passwords (e.g. "AdminPass123!", "StudentPass123!") and these credentials are printed to stdout at the end of seeding (lines 243-245).
